title: --acceptance-criteria silently clears every checked box when given a string array, and the object form that preserves them is documented only in a usage error
description:
Found 2026-09-15 while amending one acceptance criterion on QCLI-307, by measuring rather than by reading the code.

`quest task edit <id> --acceptance-criteria` accepts EITHER a JSON array of strings OR an array of `{index,text,checked}` objects. The object form preserves checked state and is the only way to amend one criterion's text without losing the others. The string form silently clears every box.

MEASURED in a throwaway workspace, three criteria with positions 1 and 3 checked:

  string array, one text amended       both checked items SILENTLY reset to false,
                                       envelope returns kind=task.updated, no warning
  objects without `index`              exit 2 usage: "--acceptance-criteria must be a
                                       JSON array of strings or {index,text,checked} items."
  objects with {index,text,checked}    one text amended, both checked states preserved

TWO DEFECTS, and they compound:

1. DISCOVERABILITY. The object form appears in exactly one place in the CLI's own output -- the usage error above. `quest manifest --json` describes the flag as `{"value":"json-array"}` and nothing more. `quest help task edit`'s summary explains --check-ac/--uncheck-ac/--remove-ac and the 1-based position vs 0-based index distinction at length and never mentions that --acceptance-criteria takes objects. So an agent reading the manifest -- which is what `quest instructions overview` tells it to read for the command contract -- concludes the flag takes strings, and is wrong.

2. SILENT DESTRUCTION. The string form is a reasonable thing to reach for and it destroys state with no signal. A caller who does not read the record back cannot tell. This is worse than the discoverability gap on its own, because the two combine into: the documented-looking path silently loses data, and the safe path is documented only on the failure branch.

WHY THIS IS WORTH FIXING RATHER THAN DOCUMENTING. This repository's own CLAUDE.md warns against inferring a fact from a neighbouring one instead of measuring it. The session that found this had recorded that warning in a tracker note in the same hour, then read `"value":"json-array"`, inferred "array of strings", and wrote the inference into a task note as though it were measured -- caught only by probing the flag before filing. A warning did not prevent it; a manifest that named the shape would have.

Not urgent: no data is known to have been lost, and QCLI-307's own amendment was made correctly with the object form. Filing so the next caller does not have to discover it the same way.

acceptanceCriteria.text: quest manifest --json describes --acceptance-criteria (and --definition-of-done, which shares the shape) in a form a caller can act on without triggering a usage error first -- the object alternative is discoverable from the machine contract, not only from the failure path
quest help task edit names the {index,text,checked} form in its prose, alongside the existing position-vs-index explanation

The string form no longer silently clears checked state: it either preserves it by matching on position, or it is refused with a message naming the object form -- decided deliberately and recorded, not left to whichever is easier

Proven both ways as two separate runs: a string-array edit behaves as decided, and an object-array edit amends one entry with every other checked state preserved, each verified by reading the record back rather than by the command's exit code

implementationNotes:
SECOND INDEPENDENT INSTANCE, SAME EVENING, DIFFERENT REPOSITORY. This raises the severity and it changes the diagnosis.

opum-agent reported 2026-09-15 23:40Z that it used the string form of --acceptance-criteria that same night, on OPAG-148, to add a fifth criterion to one of its own tasks. It did not know the object form existed and states it would have had no way to find out. It escaped loss only because all five criteria happened to be unchecked at the time -- it read the record back to confirm: 5 criteria, 0 checked, nothing lost. Its own word for that is luck, not care.

So within a few hours, two sessions in two repositories independently reached for the same lossy form, neither knowing the lossless one existed. ONE CALLER REACHING FOR THE DESTRUCTIVE PATH IS A CALLER MISTAKE; TWO INDEPENDENT CALLERS REACHING FOR IT IS THE DISCOVERABLE PATH BEING THE DESTRUCTIVE ONE. The string form is what the machine contract advertises, and it is the one that destroys state.

WHAT THIS CHANGES IN THE FIX, and it is not just a priority bump. The third criterion offers a choice -- preserve checked state by position, or refuse the string form with a message naming the object form -- and this instance argues against leaving that open much longer, because BOTH observed callers were agents reading `quest manifest --json` to learn the contract. An agent cannot be told to prefer the object form by a convention it never reads. The manifest criterion is therefore the load-bearing one; the help-text criterion is for humans and is secondary to it.

IT ALSO NARROWS THE BLAST RADIUS QUESTION. Two instances, zero actual losses, both by the same accident: the criteria involved were unchecked. That is worth stating precisely rather than dramatising -- the flag has not been shown to have lost data, only to be unable to signal when it does. The severity is in the silence and the advertising, not in a known loss.

Not folded into this task's description, which records the original discovery as it happened. A second instance reported by a third party belongs in the notes with its date and its source.

--definition-of-done MEASURED, no longer inferred. Criterion 1 named it as "which shares the shape" and that was an inference; the first note in this task hedged it correctly as "I have not probed it separately, so treat that as inferred, not measured", and then the criterion asserted it anyway. Same session, same hour, and the assertion is the one that would have been read as fact.

Caught by opum-cli-e2e, who noticed they were about to relay the inferred claim onward as confirmed and declined -- then pointed out that the criterion had already done what they had just refused to do. The relay was stopped one hop downstream; the hardened version was already upstream of it.

MEASURED in a throwaway workspace, three items with positions 1 and 3 checked:
  string array, one text amended       both checked items SILENTLY reset to false
  objects with {index,text,checked}    one text amended, both checked states preserved
Identical to --acceptance-criteria in both directions. Criterion 1 now rests on a measurement.

TWO THINGS FROM opum-cli-e2e WORTH KEEPING.

1. The manifest fix alone does not close this, and their reason is better than my criterion's. `{"value":"json-array"}` becoming `{"value":"json-array<{index,text,checked}>"}` fixes the SHAPE and says nothing about the destructive semantics of the other accepted form. A caller reading the improved manifest learns the object form exists; they do not learn the string form drops state. So a better manifest makes the trap RARER WITHOUT MAKING IT VISIBLE, and rarer-but-silent is the profile that produces the long-lived defect. Criterion 3 already asks for the refuse-or-preserve decision to be made deliberately; this argues specifically for REFUSE, because a silent preserve still never tells the caller what they nearly did.

2. They separated two candidate tests that I had collapsed into one. A RECORDS row edits one criterion's text and asserts the others' checked states survived -- the regression test for this task. A CONTRACT row asserts that a mutating command's success envelope can express what it did, because `kind=task.updated` plus exit 0 is emitted identically for a lossless and a lossy edit. The second is the bigger claim and recurs independently of this flag. They have not filed either yet, deliberately, having four open records from tonight already; they will route the id.

They also confirmed the object form from the consumer side incidentally rather than deliberately -- their TASK-74 edit preserved all three checked states, verified by re-reading the record rather than trusting the envelope -- and reported they had been about to pass a string array, on the same reasoning: the manifest says json-array and `quest help task edit` never mentions the object form. That is a THIRD independent caller reaching for the lossy form, after this session and opum-agent.

IMPLEMENTED per DEC-5, which is where the design call and the alternatives weighed are recorded.

THE RULE AS SHIPPED, and it is not the rule I wrote first. A checklist replacement is refused if and only if a currently-checked position is replaced by a BARE STRING. The test is on what the replacement CARRIES, not on the outcome.

I first wrote it as an outcome test -- refuse whenever a ticked box ends up unticked -- which reads as equivalent and is not. It refuses the DELIBERATE reset too, and the deliberate reset via the object form with checked:false is the entire escape hatch DEC-5 rests on for not adding a --force flag. So the first version quietly removed the only way to express a reset, while looking like a stricter version of the same idea. Caught by RUNNING the deliberate-reset case in a throwaway workspace, not by re-reading the rule, which had looked obviously correct both times I read it.

That is worth more than the fix: a rule stated as an invariant over OUTCOMES and a rule stated as an invariant over what the INPUT CARRIES can agree on every case you think of and differ on the one that matters. The probe found it in one run; no amount of re-reading was going to.

MEASURED, six cases, each read back from the record rather than trusted from an exit code:
  nothing checked, string form                accepted, exit 0        (no regression)
  checked list, string form                   REFUSED, exit 6, validation, record UNCHANGED
  checked list, object form amending one      accepted, other boxes preserved
  checked list, object form checked:false     accepted, reset honoured
  --definition-of-done, both directions       identical to --acceptance-criteria
  --plan                                      untouched, still a plain string array

EXIT 6 NOT 2, deliberately. The two neighbouring conflicts in the same fold (check_operation_conflict, check_index_conflict) map to usage/exit 2 because they are decided by the flag combination alone. This one depends on the record state -- the identical command line succeeds against a list with nothing ticked -- so a caller can tell "I combined flags wrongly" from "the record holds state my replacement would destroy" by exit code, without parsing prose. Follows DEC-2.

DISCOVERABILITY, both halves, because opum-cli-e2e was right that either alone is insufficient:
  manifest   --acceptance-criteria/--definition-of-done now carry items: "string | {index,text,checked}". ADDITIVE -- value stays "json-array", so a consumer switching on it is unaffected. Widening the ParameterValue union would have been tidier-looking and would break any consumer matching it exhaustively.
  help       the task edit summary now names the object form, says only it carries checked state, states the exit-6 refusal, and points at --check-ac for a one-entry change. The flag list renders --acceptance-criteria <json-array: string | {index,text,checked}> so the shape sits beside the flag, not only in prose.

MUTATION MATRIX, naming WHICH test died rather than only counts -- the QCLI-317 lesson applied here:
  guard call removed          4 pass / 2 fail   the two refusal tests (ac and dod)
  outcome-based rule restored 5 pass / 1 fail   exactly "a deliberate reset ... is honoured"
The second is the regression test for the fix-to-the-fix, and it dies alone, which is what says it is testing its own property and not riding on a neighbour.

ONE EXISTING TEST CHANGED, and it is worth being explicit that this is not a test bent to fit. qcli266 asserted `- --acceptance-criteria <json-array>` in the help flag list. Its stated intent is "help flags carry their value shape"; the shape got MORE precise for the two checklist flags, so the assertion moved with it and now also asserts that --plan still renders bare <json-array>, which is what keeps it from being a blanket rewording.

Full bun run check: 528 pass, 0 fail, 4440 expect() calls, 61 files, exit 0.

A FOURTH INDEPENDENT CALLER, and it is the strongest evidence in this record because nobody went looking for it.

opum-cli-e2e found it while sweeping PR #148 and asked that it be recorded here rather than in their own tracker, on the grounds that it is not a fact about their harness -- it is evidence about THIS defect. Attributed to them; TASK-79 on their side links rather than restates.

suites/45-parity-backlog.mjs:422 passes a BARE STRING ARRAY to task edit --acceptance-criteria, three lines above a --check-ac 1 on the same task. It survives PR #148 only on ORDER: closedTask is created at :397 with no criteria, so :422 replaces an EMPTY list -- the unchanged case -- and :423 ticks afterwards with no replacement following it. Had those two lines been written in the other order, that row would return exit 6 against this change.

WHY THIS IS WORTH MORE THAN THE THREE INSTANCES ALREADY IN THIS RECORD. Those three were sessions reaching for the lossy form live, in a hurry, and each one is answerable with "read the manual". This is COMMITTED, REVIEWED CODE in the fleet qualification harness, written by a repository whose entire job is knowing this CLI contract, sitting three lines from the very flag that would have made it lossless. Nobody was rushing. The lossy form is simply what a well-informed author reaches for, and the only thing standing between that file and silent data loss was the order of two adjacent lines.

That is "the discoverable path is the destructive one" measured in a fourth repository, in the one place least likely to get it wrong. It is also the sharpest available argument that documenting the object form would not have been enough: the author of :422 had every reason to know, and the manifest still told them the flag takes an array.

The refusal shipped in this task is what converts that latent line from silent loss into an exit 6 naming the object form. It does not need :422 to be edited.
finalSummary:
quest task edit --acceptance-criteria and --definition-of-done given a JSON array of BARE STRINGS silently cleared every checked box: exit 0, empty stderr, kind=task.updated. Landed as PR #148, squash-merged to dev as 8f474ef. Design call recorded as DEC-5.

THE RULE. Refused if and only if a currently-checked position is replaced by a bare string. The test is on what the replacement CARRIES, not on the outcome -- an entry saying checked:false has stated its intent and is honoured; a bare string has said nothing about the box. No new flag: the object form with checked:false is the deliberate-reset spelling and the refusal names it, closing the discoverability gap at the one moment the caller is certainly reading. Exit 6 validation rather than exit 2 usage, because the identical command line succeeds against a list with nothing ticked -- so a caller separates flag-misuse from record-state-conflict by exit code alone, without parsing prose.

VERIFIED, six cases, each read back from the record rather than trusted from an exit code: string form over an unchecked list still accepted; string form over a checked list refused with the record unchanged; object form amends one entry preserving the others; object form with checked:false resets; --definition-of-done identical in both directions; --plan untouched. Mutation matrix naming which test died: removing the guard kills both refusal tests, and restoring the outcome-based rule kills exactly the deliberate-reset test, alone. Full check 534 pass / 0 fail, exit 0.

BOTH DISCOVERABILITY HALVES, per opum-cli-e2e argument that either alone is insufficient -- naming the object shape fixes the SHAPE and says nothing about the other form dropping state, so a better manifest alone makes the trap rarer without making it visible, and rarer-but-silent is the profile that produces a long-lived defect. The manifest now carries items: "string | {index,text,checked}" ADDITIVELY, value staying "json-array" so a consumer switching on it is unaffected; help names the object form, the refusal, and --check-ac for a one-entry change.

WHAT NEARLY SHIPPED WRONG, and it is the transferable part. I wrote the rule as an OUTCOME test first -- refuse whenever a ticked box ends up unticked. It reads as equivalent and is not: it refuses the deliberate reset too, which silently removes the only way to express one and therefore deletes the escape hatch the no-new-flag decision rests on. Caught by RUNNING the discriminating case, not by re-reading the rule, which looked obviously correct both times. A rule stated over outcomes and a rule stated over what the input carries agree on every case you think of and differ on the one that matters.

FOUR INDEPENDENT CALLERS REACHED FOR THE LOSSY FORM, the fourth found after the fix was written and the strongest of them: committed, reviewed code in the fleet qualification harness, three lines above the flag that would have made it lossless, surviving only on the order of two adjacent lines. Nobody was rushing and the author knew the contract. That is the clearest evidence that documentation alone would not have closed this, and it is why the fix is a refusal rather than a better manual.

opum-cli-e2e contract claim is NOT closed by this and should not be read as closed: the envelope still emits kind=task.updated and exit 0 identically for a lossless and a lossy edit in every case the new rule does not refuse. That is their row to file and it recurs independently of this flag.
